Effect
ef-FEKT
n.
From Latin effectus, from efficere, to work out, to accomplish, from ex and facere, to do. Webster 1828: that which is produced by an agent or cause. The Authorized Version’s recurring phrase is of none effect — a thing rendered powerless without being formally denied.

Biblical Definition

Three times the New Testament warns that something may be made of none effect, and in each case the thing voided is precious. Our Lord names tradition as the agent: Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye (Mark 7:13). The scribes had not repealed the fifth commandment; they had built a rule about Corban that let a man evade it while appearing devout. Paul names law-keeping as the agent against promise: if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect (Romans 4:14) — inheritance by law and inheritance by promise cannot both stand, because they run on opposite principles. And he names his own eloquence as a possible agent against the cross: Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect (1 Corinthians 1:17). Against these Isaiah sets the positive: the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever (Isaiah 32:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines EFFECT as that which is produced by an agent or cause; the event which follows immediately from an antecedent cause; consequence; result; also, purpose, general intent, or reality as opposed to appearance.

EFFECT, n. — That which is produced by an agent or cause; the event which follows immediately from an antecedent cause.

Purpose; general intent; as, to this effect he spoke.

Consequence intended; utility; profit; advantage.

Reality; not mere appearance; as, in effect it is the same thing.

Latin effectus, from efficio, from ex and facio, to make — the root of efficient and efficacious.

Key Scripture

Mark 7:13 — "Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye."

Romans 4:14 — "For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect:"

1 Corinthians 1:17 — "For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect."

Isaiah 32:17 — "And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever."

Modern Corruption

Mark 7:13 shows Scripture voided not by denial but by tradition laid alongside it, which is precisely the mechanism the Reformation identified in Rome and which no communion is immune to.

expand to see more

The scribes did not deny Honour thy father and thy mother; they added a rule that let a man declare his property Corban, a gift devoted to God, and so escape the duty while gaining a reputation for piety. The commandment stood on the page and was dead in practice. This is the essential Reformation argument against the elevation of tradition to a coordinate authority with Scripture: what is added does not merely supplement, it eventually overrules. Trent’s decree receiving unwritten traditions with equal affection and reverence as the written books is the formal version of the error our Lord names here. But no communion is safe from it. Wherever a confessional church allows a custom, a founder’s practice, or a house rule to become functionally unquestionable, the mechanism of Mark 7:13 is at work, and sola Scriptura is the standing remedy.

1 Corinthians 1:17 is the verse most often needed in the pulpit and least often applied. Paul feared that his own wisdom of words could empty the cross of its power — not contradict it, but void it, by shifting the hearer’s attention from the message to the performance. The modern equivalents are not eloquence alone but production, personality, and the sermon built to be memorable rather than to be true. The chapter’s argument is that God deliberately chose the foolishness of preaching and the offence of a crucified Messiah so that no flesh should glory in His presence. A ministry that succeeds by the very means Paul refused has not thereby proved him wrong; it has made the cross of none effect and called the result fruit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek akuroo (G208), to make void, to deprive of authority; kenoo (G2758), to empty; katargeo (G2673), to render inoperative; Hebrew abodah (H5656), work or service.

expand to see more

Greek akuroo (G208) — to deprive of force or authority, to make void; making the word of God of none effect (Mark 7:13).

Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render idle or inoperative; the promise made of none effect (Romans 4:14).

Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty out; lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect (1 Corinthians 1:17).

Greek korban (G2878) — a gift devoted to God; the device by which the commandment was evaded (Mark 7:11).

Hebrew abodah (H5656) — work, service, the thing wrought; the effect of righteousness (Isaiah 32:17).

Usage

"Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition (Mark 7:13) — the commandment left on the page and dead in practice."

"The promise made of none effect (Romans 4:14) — law and promise run on opposite principles and cannot both be the ground."

"Lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect (1 Corinthians 1:17) — Paul’s fear of his own eloquence."
